<objective>
Close the device-lifecycle and test-integrity warnings: the 10-year cookie that never gets
cleared (WR-05), the cookie written before the swap that may fail (WR-06), the discarded
cleanup result (WR-08), the completed revoke reported as a failure (WR-09), and the denial
assertions that assert nothing when the query errors (WR-13). Then record the info-level
findings and close the phase gate.

**As a** restaurant owner who has just revoked a lost tablet, **I want to** see that it
worked and not be signed out of my own browser every three minutes afterwards, **so that**
the safety valve is something I can actually use under pressure.

Purpose: `cena_device_user` is set with a ten-year `maxAge` and is never deleted by
anything — not revoke, not exit-owner-mode, not sign-out. A browser that once ran
`enableStaffMode` and had the swap fail, or whose device was later revoked, gets
`signOut()` plus a redirect to `/login` every three idle minutes forever with no UI to
clear it. And the two most consequential failure paths in `lib/devices.ts` both lie: one
discards the result of the cleanup it exists to perform, the other reports a revocation
that fully landed as "Something went wrong".

Output: a device cookie with a lifecycle, two honest failure paths, a denial-shape helper
used across the RLS suite, and the phase's final gate.
</objective>

    - A staff-mode-enabled event whose swap FAILED yields an empty directive list — no set-device directive at all.

    - An owner-unlock-exit with outcome "no-device-cookie" yields delete directives for BOTH the device and the staff cookie.
    - An owner-unlock-exit with outcome "device-not-active" yields delete directives for BOTH cookies. This is the revoked-tablet case that produces the three-minute logout loop.
    - An owner-unlock-exit with outcome "no-session", "rotation-failed" or "swap-back-failed" yields an EMPTY directive list — each is recoverable and the device is still legitimately enrolled, so clearing the cookie would force a manual re-enrolment for a transient error.
    - An owner-unlock-exit with outcome "already-device" yields an empty directive list.
    - An owner-unlock-exit with outcome "swapped-back" yields exactly a delete-staff directive and no device directive, preserving the tablet's identity while clearing whoever last entered a PIN.

    - A browser-unenrolled event yields delete directives for both cookies.

  </behavior>
  <action>
    **Extract the decision, not the cookie I/O.** The defects here are decisions — *whether* to
    write the cookie and *when* to clear it — living inside a Server Action that cannot be
    imported under Vitest. Proving a line moved is not proving the decision changed, which is
    the same shape of evidence that let CR-01 ship behind a green suite. So the decision moves
    into a Next-free module first, exactly as plan 01-06 did for owner authority.

    Create `lib/device-cookie-policy.ts`, importing nothing from `next/*`. Export a
    discriminated-union input type `DeviceCookieEvent` with these members:
    `{ kind: "staff-mode-enabled"; swapFailed: boolean }`;
    `{ kind: "owner-unlock-exit"; outcome: "no-device-cookie" | "no-session" | "already-device" | "device-not-active" | "rotation-failed" | "swap-back-failed" | "swapped-back" }`;
    `{ kind: "device-revoked"; revokedDeviceUserId: string; thisBrowserDeviceUserId: string | null }`;
    and `{ kind: "browser-unenrolled" }`. Export an output type
    `CookieDirective = { op: "set"; cookie: "device" } | { op: "delete"; cookie: "device" | "staff" }`
    and the function `deviceCookieDirectives(event: DeviceCookieEvent): CookieDirective[]`
    implementing exactly the table in `&lt;behavior&gt;`.

    Give the module a header comment stating the policy's one organising rule: a cookie is
    cleared when the browser is PROVABLY no longer this tablet, and never for a failure that
    is merely transient. That distinction is load-bearing and is why three of the seven
    owner-unlock-exit outcomes return nothing: "no-session", "rotation-failed" and
    "swap-back-failed" all leave a device whose registry row is still active, so clearing the
    cookie would cost the venue a manual re-enrolment in exchange for nothing. Only
    "no-device-cookie" (the value does not decode, so this browser cannot prove it is any
    tablet) and "device-not-active" (no live `venue_devices` row, so the device is revoked or
    belongs to another venue) are terminal.

    **WR-06 — set the cookie only after the swap succeeds.** In `enableStaffMode`, move the
    `cookieStore.set(DEVICE_COOKIE_NAME, ...)` call and the `cookieStore.delete(STAFF_COOKIE_NAME)`
    call so both run AFTER `signInWithPassword` has returned without an error. The swap-error
    branch must return `COPY.devices.swapFailed` with no device cookie written at all.
    Today the cookie is written first, so a transient network failure leaves the browser
    permanently branded as that tablet while still holding the OWNER's session — and
    `DashboardLayout` then mounts `IdleRelock`, so three idle minutes later `exitOwnerUnlock`
    rotates the device password and swaps the owner into a staff session, silently converting
    the owner's laptop into the tablet. Add a comment recording that ordering is the whole
    fix and that the branding must never outlive a failed swap.

    **WR-05 — clear the cookies through the policy, and only where the policy says to.**
    In `exitOwnerUnlock`, every branch must classify itself into one of the seven
    `owner-unlock-exit` outcomes, call `deviceCookieDirectives`, and apply whatever comes back
    before it signs out or redirects. No branch may decide for itself which cookies to touch;
    the policy module is the only place that decision exists.

    The case that matters is `device-not-active`. Leaving the cookie there means
    `DashboardLayout` keeps mounting `IdleRelock` on a browser whose device has been revoked,
    so `exitOwnerUnlock` finds no active row, signs out and redirects to `/login` — every three
    idle minutes, forever, with no UI to stop it. Clearing the cookie is what breaks that loop.

    In `revokeDevice`, after `revokeDeviceById` returns, build a `device-revoked` event from its
    `deviceUserId` and from `decodeDeviceCookie` of this request's own `DEVICE_COOKIE_NAME`,
    call the policy, and apply the result. When they match, the owner just revoked the browser
    they are sitting at and it must not keep believing it is a tablet; when they do not, this
    request's browser is untouched.

    Add a helper in `actions/devices.ts` that takes a `CookieDirective[]` and the cookie store
    and performs the set or delete for each, mapping `"device"` to `DEVICE_COOKIE_NAME` and
    `"staff"` to `STAFF_COOKIE_NAME` and carrying the existing cookie options
    (`httpOnly`, `sameSite: "lax"`, `path: "/"`, `secure` in production,
    `maxAge: DEVICE_COOKIE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS`). Keeping the mapping in one place is what stops a
    future branch from quietly reintroducing an ad-hoc cookie write.

    **The un-enrol affordance.** Add an exported Server Action `unenrollThisBrowser(): Promise<void>`
    to `actions/devices.ts` that deletes both cookies, calls `supabase.auth.signOut()` and
    redirects to `/login`. Document what it deliberately does NOT do: it does not revoke the
    device server-side, so the registry row stays active and the owner can still see and
    revoke it from the dashboard. This is the local equivalent of clearing cookies, not a
    privileged operation, which is why it needs no authority check — anyone who can press it
    is already holding the tablet.

    Create `app/(tablet)/components/UnenrollBrowserButton.tsx` as a client component mirroring
    `ExitOwnerModeButton`: `useTransition`, disabled while pending, a `Loader2` spinner, and
    every string from `COPY`. Use the `ghost` variant — un-enrolling loses nothing that cannot
    be redone by enabling staff mode again, so the UI-SPEC colour rule that reserves
    destructive styling for revoke and deactivate applies.

    Render it in `app/(tablet)/unlock/page.tsx` in BOTH branches where `deviceUserId` is
    non-null — the owner-mode branch and the login-form branch — so a tablet stuck in the
    revoked-device loop has a way out from whichever screen it lands on. Leave the
    `!deviceUserId` branch alone: there is nothing to un-enrol there.

    Add the copy keys this needs to `lib/copy.ts` under `ownerUnlock`: a label for the control
    and a one-line explanation that un-enrolling only affects this browser and does not revoke
    the device for the venue. Follow the file's existing convention of a comment above any key
    whose wording is load-bearing.

    Create `tests/lib/device-cookie-policy.test.ts` covering every case in `&lt;behavior&gt;`. It is
    a pure module, so the file needs no fixtures and no running stack. Assert the returned
    directive ARRAYS with `toEqual`, not merely their length — a policy that returns the right
    number of wrong directives must go red. Enumerate all seven `owner-unlock-exit` outcomes
    explicitly rather than looping over a list, so a future outcome added to the union without
    a test is visible as an absent case.

    Write the swap-failed case and the `device-not-active` case RED first, against a stub
    policy that returns an empty list for everything, and confirm each fails for the right
    reason before implementing the table.
  </action>

  <read_first>

The reconcile block at lines 162-168 discards the `deleteUser` result (WR-08); `revokeDeviceById` calls `rotateDevicePassword` at line 246 after both real revocation steps have already committed (WR-09), and its doc comment at lines 178-200 explicitly frames rotation as defence in depth on top of the real revocation.

  <files>lib/devices.ts, actions/devices.ts, tests/lib/device-failure-paths.test.ts</files>
  <behavior>
    - When the venue_members insert inside enrollDevice fails and the subsequent deleteUser also fails, enrollDevice throws once, and the thrown message contains the orphaned auth user id, the original failure text and the cleanup failure text.
    - When the venue_members insert fails and deleteUser succeeds, enrollDevice rethrows the original error and the auth user no longer exists.
    - When rotateDevicePassword throws during revokeDeviceById, the call still returns revoked true with the device's user id and venue id, the venue_members row is gone, and revoked_at is stamped.
    - The device principal reads zero venue_members rows after that partially-failed revoke, so the revocation is real regardless of the rotation.
    - A second revoke of the same device returns revoked false and changes nothing.
  </behavior>
  <action>
    **WR-08 — stop discarding the cleanup result.** The Supabase admin client does not throw on
    API errors; it returns a result object. In `enrollDevice`'s catch block, destructure the
    error from `admin.auth.admin.deleteUser(deviceUserId)`. When it is non-null, throw a NEW
    Error whose message names `enrollDevice`, states that provisioning failed AND cleanup
    failed, and includes the orphaned `deviceUserId`, the original error's message and the
    cleanup error's message. When it is null, rethrow the original error unchanged so the
    existing behaviour is preserved. An orphaned auth user is a member of nothing and is
    therefore invisible to every screen in the product — which is exactly the state the
    reconcile block exists to prevent, so its failure must be loud and must carry the id a
    human needs to clean it up by hand.

    While in `actions/devices.ts`, correct the comment in `enableStaffMode`'s catch that
    asserts there is never a half-provisioned principal left behind. Say what is now true:
    enrolment reconciles its own partial state and, when the reconcile itself fails, throws an
    error naming the orphan rather than hiding it.

    **WR-09 — a completed revoke is never reported as a failure.** In `revokeDeviceById`, wrap
    the `rotateDevicePassword` call in try/catch. On failure, `console.error` with a message
    naming the device user id and stating that the revocation itself already landed, then
    continue to the normal return. Do not rethrow. Both real revocation steps — deleting the
    `venue_members` row, which RLS re-resolves on every query, and stamping `revoked_at` — have

<threat_model>
## Trust Boundaries

| Boundary | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| tablet browser -> device cookie lifecycle | A ten-year cookie decides whether `IdleRelock` mounts and whether `exitOwnerUnlock` will try to swap this browser into a staff session. |
| Server Action -> service-role client | `enrollDevice` and `revokeDeviceById` run with RLS bypassed; their failure paths decide whether privileged state is left inconsistent. |
| test suite -> release gate | The RLS suite is D-25's release gate. An assertion that passes vacuously is a boundary that reports itself as verified while unverified. |

## STRIDE Threat Register

| Threat ID | Category | Component | Severity | Disposition | Mitigation Plan |
|-----------|----------|-----------|----------|-------------|-----------------|
| T-01G-26 | Denial of Service | `cena_device_user` lifecycle | high | mitigate | WR-05: nothing deletes the cookie, so a browser whose device was revoked signs itself out every three idle minutes forever with no UI to clear it. Task 1 moves the decision into `deviceCookieDirectives` and clears both cookies for the two outcomes that prove the browser is no longer a tablet (`no-device-cookie`, `device-not-active`), on a matching self-revoke, and through the new un-enrol control. Proven by a unit test asserting the directive arrays with `toEqual`, not by counting delete calls. |
| T-01G-26b | Denial of Service | over-eager cookie clearing | medium | mitigate | The obvious reading of WR-05 — "clear on every terminal path" — would also clear on `no-session`, `rotation-failed` and `swap-back-failed`, each of which leaves a device whose registry row is still active. That trades a logout loop for a manual re-enrolment on a transient error. The policy returns an empty list for all three, and the test asserts it. |
| T-01G-27 | Elevation of Privilege | `enableStaffMode` cookie ordering | high | mitigate | WR-06: the cookie is written before the swap that may fail, leaving the owner's own machine branded as the tablet while still holding the owner's session — after which the idle timer converts it into a staff device. Task 1 asserts the behavior directly: a `staff-mode-enabled` event with `swapFailed: true` returns `[]`, so no set-device directive exists for the failure path at all. The line-ordering `awk` gate is retained only as a secondary structural check. |
| T-01G-28 | Repudiation | `enrollDevice` reconcile | medium | mitigate | WR-08: the `deleteUser` result is discarded, so a failed cleanup leaves an orphaned auth user that is a member of nothing and is therefore invisible to every screen in the product. Task 2 throws a compound error carrying the orphan's id so a human can find it. |
| T-01G-29 | Denial of Service | `revokeDeviceById` rotation | high | mitigate | WR-09: a rotation failure propagates and the owner is told a fully-effective revocation failed, and `revalidatePath` never runs — during the lost-tablet panic the feature exists for. Task 2 logs and continues, because both real revocation steps have already committed. Proven by a test that forces the rotation failure and asserts the membership row is gone anyway. |
| T-01G-30 | Tampering | RLS denial assertions | high | mitigate | WR-13: `if (error === null) { expect(...) }` asserts nothing when the query errors, so a renamed column or a dropped RPC turns the release gate green. Task 3 adds `expectDenialError` at every site and requires the helper be observed failing against a deliberately broken probe before the task is done. |
| T-01G-31 | Information Disclosure | `unenrollThisBrowser` | low | accept | The new action clears cookies and signs out with no authority check. Accepted: it is reachable only from a browser that already holds the tablet, it grants nothing, and it does not revoke the device server-side — the registry row stays active and visible to the owner. Equivalent in effect to the user clearing their own cookies. |
| T-01G-32 | Spoofing | shared HMAC key across device and staff cookies (IN-01) | low | accept | Carried from 01-06. Recorded in `deferred-items.md` in Task 3 with the concrete resolution, and pinned by an explicit test so the behaviour cannot change unnoticed. |
</threat_model>
